## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

# Handoff — memory-tier lint (`memlint.py`) and memory cleanup

Written 2026-09-02. Session ran on 2026-09-01 evening as a background job.
Machine: macOS. Working directory: `~/DEV`.

## What the session was asked to do

1. Watch a YouTube video and decide what applies to this Claude Code system.
   Video: "This Fixes Claude's Biggest Problem (Karpathy's Method)", Austin
   Marchese, 18:02 — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4hIvG849w4Y
2. Then, on Eric's pick, act on the top finding.

## Where the analysis lives — do not re-derive it

- **Video review + gap analysis + what was done:**
  `~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-01-dream-video-review.md`
  Covers what the video builds, what this system already had, the three gaps
  found, and the full cleanup log. Read this first.
- **Latest lint output:**
  `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/reports/memlint-2026-09-01.md`
- **Tool docs:** `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/AGENTS.md`, section
  "memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks". Also summarised in `README.md`.
- **Archive provenance:** a `README.md` sits in each `_archive/` folder naming
  what superseded each retired memory.

## What was built

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/scripts/memlint.py` — new. Lints the memory
tier, which `lint.py` never touched: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the active
`~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Six checks; reports only, never edits a
memory file. Wired to run after the Sunday 02:30 adjudication job.

Supporting changes in the same repo (`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler`, a git
repo): `scripts/config.py` (memory-tier paths, retired-slug exclusion),
`scripts/weekly-adjudicate.ps1` (runs memlint after adjudicate.py), `README.md`,
`AGENTS.md`.

**These changes are uncommitted.** `git status` in that repo also shows
pre-existing modifications to `hooks/session-start.py`, `scripts/flush.py` and
`uv.lock` that this session did not make — do not sweep those into a commit
without checking with Eric.

## Result

Contradictions found by the LLM check went 34 → 17 after cleanup. Twelve memory
files were corrected in place; five were archived (not deleted) with their index
pointers removed. Details in the vault note above.

## Design decisions worth not re-litigating

- **Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere.** The macOS
  slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as
  duplication (~30 false pairs). `config.RETIRED_SLUG_PREFIX`.
- **Near-duplicate threshold is 0.45, measured not guessed.** On the real corpus
  the highest genuine within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints top
  pairs per slug so the number can be retuned against evidence.
- **Similarity is within-slug only.** Cross-slug pairs are noise by design.
- **`--structural-only` writes `memlint-<date>-structural.md`**, so a free run
  cannot clobber the day's paid-for LLM findings. This was a real footgun hit
  three times before it was fixed.
- **Report-only is deliberate.** Eric's memory records a permission gate on
  acting unasked, and `memory-write` requires confirmation before deleting.

## Open items

1. **Commit the compiler changes** if Eric wants them committed. Not done —
   he did not ask.
2. **Compiler backlog.** Flagged again at session start on 2026-09-02:
   `compiler-backlog: 7 log(s) backlogged, compiling newest 2 this run`.
   Fix: `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/compile.py`
3. **memsearch ETIMEDOUT streak**, 6x then 7x, logged 2026-09-02 ~02:50–02:57.
   A new memory `project_memsearch-hook-timeout-cap.md` appeared in the DEV
   index after this session ended, so another session may already be on it —
   check before duplicating work. Per `keystoneos-verification-habits`, a
   timeout streak is expected noise below a threshold of 6; at 7 it is worth a
   look, not an alarm.
4. **Four memory files Eric deliberately kept**, which account for roughly half
   the 17 remaining conflicts. He chose to keep them rather than archive; do not
   archive them without asking again:
   `~/.claude/projects/-Users-kristinarash/memory/reference_secondbrain-backup.md`,
   `reference_okr-staff-meeting-prep.md`, `project_catapult_cli.md`,
   `project_zotero_cli.md`.
5. **Two FaceComps files in the `~` slug** duplicate each other and disagree on
   a staff member's surname. Needs Eric's domain knowledge, not a linter.
   `project_facecomps-practice-simulator.md` vs `project_practice-load-framework.md`.
6. **Naming inconsistency in memory frontmatter.** Some files declare
   `name: project-foo`, others `name: foo`, while `MEMORY.md` links
   `project_foo.md`. This causes ~23 broken `[[links]]` that memlint reports as
   auto-fixable. Fixing them is *not* mechanical — Eric has to pick the
   canonical form first. He was offered this and chose the memory cleanup
   instead. Do not "fix" links by guessing; one such guess broke a working link
   during this session and had to be reverted.

## Two gaps found but not built

From the video review, still open (detail in the vault note):

- **`session-miner` reads summaries, not the record.** Its sources are
  `global-memory/transcripts/*.md` and compiler `daily/*.md`, last 7 days. The
  raw record is ~400 `.jsonl` files (~360 MB) in `~/.claude/projects/` that
  nothing mines. Trawl in a subagent if this is picked up.
- **Proposals evaporate.** `improve-system` and `session-miner` propose and stop
  by design, but a proposal made in a session that ends is lost. A pending file
  that the next run reads first would keep the approval gate and stop the loss.

## How to run the tool

```bash
cd ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler
uv run --directory . python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only   # free
uv run --directory . python scripts/memlint.py                     # + LLM check
uv run --directory . python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs         # wider LLM scope
```

`uv` is at `/Users/kristinarash/.local/bin/uv` — a standalone install, not
Homebrew. Do not relocate it.

## Environment notes that cost time this session

- `timeout` is not installed on this machine (no GNU coreutils).
- The `dcg` guard blocks `rm -rf` under `$HOME` and blocks a Bash call that
  embeds a `pwsh -Command` with runtime expansion. Split such commands, or run
  the script with `pwsh -File`.
- Piping a long script's output through `tail -N` silently discarded the first
  half of a transcript early in this session. Redirect to a file instead.

  slug rules, and the retrieval ladder. **Invoke this before writing, updating

  `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/`.** It also requires user confirmation before a
  delete, which is why the archiving in this session was gated on a question.
- `claude-stack-doctor` — for items 2 and 3 above (compiler backlog, memsearch
  timeouts, launchd job health). Run this before diagnosing by hand.
- `session-miner` — if picking up the "raw `.jsonl` never mined" gap.
- `improve-system` — the vault-side equivalent of memlint; relevant if the
  "proposals evaporate" gap is picked up, since it is one of the two skills that
  proposes and stops.
- `superpowers:verification-before-completion` — this session's findings only
  held up because each LLM claim was checked against the filesystem before
  acting. Several "stale" flags turned out to be partly wrong on inspection.
- `closeout` — if the next session ends the day's work.

Do **not** reach for `graphify` or `code-review` here; nothing in this thread
needs them.

API key lives in the macOS login Keychain, not in `~/.zshrc`. The `.zshrc` line
reads it out via `security find-generic-password`. A memory file that still said

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

session-end index was timing out.** Incremental indexing had quietly degraded to "whatever
the 09:00 nightly full reindex picks up", leaving search up to 24h stale.

surfaced. It took **six session-ends inside 47 minutes** (2026-09-01, 21:09-21:56) to
produce a 7-long streak and one `.errors.log` line. The alarm fired on burst *frequency*,
never on the underlying constant failure.

done | sort | uniq -c

import os, re, collections
root = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/projects")

        if n is None: k = "NO name: field"

    print(f"{v:4d}  {k}")
    for e in examples[k]: print("        ", e)

Base directory for this skill: /Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/memory-write

# Memory Write

## Outcome
- Fact added to, updated in, or removed from the correct memory tier
- Tier-B caps enforced (2,500 chars for MEMORY.md, 1,375 for USER.md)
- Confirmation: "Saved — will be active from next session."

## Pick the tier first

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across multiple projects?"

**Tier A — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`** (one file per fact, indexed by MEMORY.md)
- Durable user facts → `user_*.md` (metadata.type: user)
- Stable project conventions / gotchas → `project_*.md` (metadata.type: project)
- Behavioral feedback rules → `feedback_*.md` (metadata.type: feedback)
- External-system pointers → `reference_*.md` (metadata.type: reference)

**Tier B — `~/.claude/global-memory/`** (single capped file)
- Active threads (in-progress work) → `MEMORY.md` `## Active Threads`
- Current env notes (URLs, tool versions, project structure in play) → `MEMORY.md` `## Environment Notes`
- Pending decisions → `MEMORY.md` `## Pending Decisions`
- Durable user profile updates → `USER.md`

## Steps

1. **Decide tier** using the rule above.
2. **Read** the target file in full.
3. **Dedup check** — substring scan; if the fact already exists, skip or update in place.
4. **Cap check** for Tier B — `wc -c < ~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (or USER.md). If over cap, consolidate (merge similar entries, prune stale) before adding.
5. **Write** the change.
   - Tier A: create a new file with proper frontmatter (name, description, metadata.type) and add a one-line pointer to that slug's `MEMORY.md` index.
   - Tier B: append under the correct `##` section.
6. **Confirm** in one line: `Saved — will be active from next session.`

## Actions

- **add** — append (default)
- **replace** — substring match + swap. Preferred over add when updating an existing fact.
- **remove** — confirm with the user before deleting.

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the retired Windows slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

## Daily compiled logs — read-only

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never hand-edit these files.** The compiler owns them.
- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## What is loaded at session start

`~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are read once at session start and are a **frozen snapshot**. Mid-session writes persist to disk but only take effect next session — this is deliberate, to preserve the prefix cache. Never load more than the startup set proactively.

## Rules

- Never exceed Tier B caps. Consolidate first.
- Always dedup before adding.
- For Tier A, the slug is the current cwd with `/` and `.` replaced by `-` (so `~` → `-Users-kristinarash`, `~/DEV` → `-Users-kristinarash-DEV`, `~/.claude/skills` → `-Users-kristinarash--claude-skills`). The harness injects the correct slug each session — use that, don't reconstruct it.
- **Never write to a `C--Users-eric-rash*` slug.** Those are pre-migration Windows keys from the box retired 2026-08-14. They are still indexed by memsearch, so old facts stay recallable, but nothing written there will ever be auto-injected again.
- Never announce the write mid-session beyond the one-line confirmation. The injected snapshot is frozen — the new fact appears next session, not this one.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Normalize memory-tier `name:` frontmatter to the bare kebab-case form
3	(Option A) and repoint every [[wikilink]] at the new canonical names.
4	
5	Canonical name = filename stem, minus a LEADING type token
6	(project|user|reference|feedback) followed by - or _, kebab-cased.
7	
8	Deliberately derived from the FILENAME, not from the existing `name:` value:
9	stripping a prefix off `feedback_project_idea_capture.md`'s declared name
10	`project-idea-capture` would wrongly yield `idea-capture`.
11	
12	Report-only unless --apply is passed.
13	"""
14	import os
15	import re
16	import sys
17	import argparse
18	
19	ROOT = os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/projects")
20	# Retired pre-migration Windows keys. Seen on disk with both `C--` and `c--`,
21	# so match case-insensitively - CLAUDE.md forbids writing to any of them.
22	RETIRED = "c--users-eric-rash"
23	TYPE_TOKEN = re.compile(r"^(project|user|reference|feedback)[-_]")
24	# `[[:space:]]` and friends are POSIX character classes sitting in shell
25	# snippets, not wikilinks. A colon never appears in a memory name.
26	NOT_A_LINK = re.compile(r"[:\s]")
27	
28	
29	def canonical(stem: str) -> str:
30	    """Filename stem -> canonical bare kebab-case name."""
31	    return TYPE_TOKEN.sub("", stem).replace("_", "-").lower()
32	
33	
34	def aliases(stem: str, declared: str | None) -> set[str]:
35	    """Every spelling a link might plausibly use for this file."""
36	    canon = canonical(stem)
37	    out = {
38	        canon,
39	        stem.lower(),
40	        stem.replace("_", "-").lower(),
41	        canon.replace("-", "_"),
42	    }
43	    for t in ("project", "user", "reference", "feedback"):
44	        out.add(f"{t}-{canon}")
45	        out.add(f"{t}_{canon}")
46	    if declared:
47	        out.add(declared.strip().strip('"').lower())
48	    return out
49	
50	
51	def slugs():
52	    for s in sorted(os.listdir(ROOT)):
53	        if s.lower().startswith(RETIRED):
54	            continue
55	        mem = os.path.join(ROOT, s, "memory")
56	        if os.path.isdir(mem):
57	            yield s, mem
58	
59	
60	def main() -> int:
61	    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
62	    ap.add_argument("--apply", action="store_true")
63	    args = ap.parse_args()
64	
65	    renames, linkfixes, unresolved, collisions = [], [], [], []
66	
67	    for slug, mem in slugs():
68	        files = [f for f in sorted(os.listdir(mem))
69	                 if f.endswith(".md") and f != "MEMORY.md"]
70	
71	        # Pass 1 - build this slug's alias -> canonical resolution map.
72	        canon_of, alias_map, texts = {}, {}, {}
73	        for fn in files:
74	            path = os.path.join(mem, fn)
75	            txt = open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace").read()
76	            texts[fn] = txt
77	            stem = fn[:-3]
78	            m = re.search(r"^name:\s*(.+)$", txt, re.M)
79	            declared = m.group(1).strip().strip('"') if m else None
80	            canon = canonical(stem)
81	            canon_of[fn] = (canon, declared)
82	            for a in aliases(stem, declared):
83	                alias_map.setdefault(a, set()).add(canon)
84	
85	        # Two files claiming the same alias -> refuse to guess.
86	        ambiguous = {a for a, v in alias_map.items() if len(v) > 1}
87	        for a in sorted(ambiguous):
88	            collisions.append(f"{slug}: alias [[{a}]] matches {sorted(alias_map[a])}")
89	
90	        valid = {c for c, _ in canon_of.values()}
91	
92	        # Pass 2 - rewrite name: and links.
93	        for fn in files:
94	            path, txt = os.path.join(mem, fn), texts[fn]
95	            canon, declared = canon_of[fn]
96	            new = txt
97	
98	            if declared is None:
99	                unresolved.append(f"{slug}/{fn}: no `name:` field - left alone")
100	            elif declared != canon:
101	                new = re.sub(r"^name:\s*.+$", f"name: {canon}", new, count=1, flags=re.M)
102	                renames.append(f"{slug}/{fn}: {declared} -> {canon}")
103	
104	            def fix(mo):
105	                target = mo.group(1).strip()
106	                if NOT_A_LINK.search(target):
107	                    return mo.group(0)
108	                key = target.lower()
109	                if key in valid:
110	                    return f"[[{key}]]" if target != key else mo.group(0)
111	                hits = alias_map.get(key, set()) - ambiguous_for(key)
112	                if len(hits) == 1:
113	                    dest = next(iter(hits))
114	                    linkfixes.append(f"{slug}/{fn}: [[{target}]] -> [[{dest}]]")
115	                    return f"[[{dest}]]"
116	                unresolved.append(f"{slug}/{fn}: [[{target}]] unresolved - left alone")
117	                return mo.group(0)
118	
119	            def ambiguous_for(key):
120	                return alias_map.get(key, set()) if key in ambiguous else set()
121	
122	            new = re.sub(r"\[\[([^\]\|]+)\]\]", fix, new)
123	
124	            if new != txt and args.apply:
125	                with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
126	                    fh.write(new)
127	
128	    def dump(title, rows):
129	        print(f"\n=== {title} ({len(rows)}) ===")
130	        for r in rows:
131	            print("  " + r)
132	
133	    dump("NAME CHANGES", renames)
134	    dump("LINK FIXES", linkfixes)
135	    dump("COLLISIONS - not touched", collisions)
136	    dump("UNRESOLVED - left alone", unresolved)
137	    print(f"\nMode: {'APPLIED' if args.apply else 'DRY RUN'}")
138	    return 0
139	
140	
141	if __name__ == "__main__":
142	    sys.exit(main())

# Session Miner

Pull uncaptured learnings out of recent session history. Data-gathering skill: it reads history and proposes destinations; the user picks.

## Sources, in order

1. `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/*.md` (last 7 days)

For anything beyond a quick scan, spawn a subagent to do the trawling and return only findings — raw transcript text should not fill the main conversation.

## What to hunt for

- **Repeated corrections** → feedback memory or a skill fix
- **Decisions with rationale** → permanent vault note
- **Discovered gotchas** → project memory
- **Workflows that worked** → skill candidate

## Output

Present findings as a checklist: each item = the learning + where it should live (memory tier, vault note, skill edit, new skill). User picks; route each approved item to its destination — use memory-write conventions for memories, capture-insight format for vault notes, write-a-skill for skill changes.

## Rules

- Report before you mutate. Nothing is written until the user approves the checklist items.
- Cite evidence (date, file) for each finding so the user can judge it.
- An empty result is legitimate — don't manufacture learnings to look thorough.

## Customization

**Before executing, check for user customizations at:**
`~/.claude/LIFEOS/USER/CUSTOMIZATIONS/SKILLS/CreateSkill/`

If this directory exists, load and apply any PREFERENCES.md, configurations, or resources found there. These override default behavior. If the directory does not exist, proceed with skill defaults.


## 🚨 MANDATORY: Voice Notification (REQUIRED BEFORE ANY ACTION)

**You MUST send this notification BEFORE doing anything else when this skill is invoked.**

1. **Send voice notification**:
   ```bash
   curl -s -X POST http://localhost:31337/notify \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"message": "Running the WORKFLOWNAME workflow in the CreateSkill skill to ACTION"}' \
     > /dev/null 2>&1 &
   ```

2. **Output text notification**:
   ```
   Running the **WorkflowName** workflow in the **CreateSkill** skill to ACTION...
   ```

**This is not optional. Execute this curl command immediately upon skill invocation.**

# CreateSkill

Complete skill development lifecycle: **structure** (create, validate, canonicalize) + **effectiveness** (test, improve, optimize triggers). Structural workflows ensure skills follow LifeOS conventions. Effectiveness workflows — inspired by Anthropic's skill-creator — ensure skills actually work and trigger reliably.

## Enforcement

Handrolling skill files — writing `SKILL.md` or `Workflows/`, `Tools/`, `References/` by hand — is forbidden by `skills/CLAUDE.md`. Spawn this skill first and let it orchestrate. Reading these workflows and performing the steps yourself is the exact anti-pattern the rule exists to prevent.

This skill is the **single home** for skill authoring here. `write-a-skill` is a pointer to it; `superpowers:writing-skills` is a third-party plugin skill and is not the authority in this workspace. (Consolidated 2026-08-15.)

*This text used to live in the frontmatter `description`. Descriptions load into every session's system prompt, so enforcement prose belongs in the body — the description now carries only what is needed to trigger.*

## Authoritative Source

**Before creating ANY skill, READ:** `~/.claude/LIFEOS/DOCUMENTATION/Skills/SkillSystem.md`

**Canonical example to follow:** any well-formed public skill in `~/.claude/skills/` (e.g. `Research/SKILL.md`, `Daemon/SKILL.md`, `CreateSkill/SKILL.md` itself).

## Naming Convention — Public vs Private

**Skill name encodes its public/private status. There are exactly two valid forms.**

| Skill type | Directory format | Example | Allowed content |
|------------|------------------|---------|-----------------|
| **Public** | `TitleCase` | `Blogging`, `Daemon`, `CreateSkill` | Templated, safe, generic, ready for public release |
| **Private** | `_ALLCAPS` (underscore prefix, all uppercase) | `<your-release-skill>`, `_INBOX`, `_BROADCAST`, `_DOTFILES` | Anything personal, sensitive, identity-bound, customer-bound, or environment-specific |

**The leading underscore is the public-release boundary.** Release tooling skips `_*` skills entirely — they never leave `~/.claude`. Public skills (no underscore) are mirrored into the LifeOS public release and MUST contain only generic, templated content.

**Sub-file naming (both public and private skills):**

| Component | Format | Example |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Workflow files | `TitleCase.md` | `Create.md`, `UpdateDaemonInfo.md` |
| Reference docs | `TitleCase.md` | `ProsodyGuide.md`, `ApiReference.md` |
| Tool files | `TitleCase.ts` | `ManageServer.ts` |
| Help files | `TitleCase.help.md` | `ManageServer.help.md` |

**Wrong (NEVER use):**
- Skill dirs: `createskill`, `create-skill`, `CREATE_SKILL` (no underscore + caps for public; no kebab/snake for private)
- Files: `create.md`, `update-info.md`, `SYNC_REPO.md`

### Choosing public vs private — the decision rule

Ask: **"Could this skill be dropped, as-is, into a stranger's `~/.claude/skills/` and just work?"**

- **Yes** → public skill (`TitleCase`). Body must be generic; user-specific config layers in via `LIFEOS/USER/CUSTOMIZATIONS/SKILLS/<SkillName>/`.
- **No, because it references my identity, my contacts, my business, my customer, my paid API, my private infra, my domain, my private repo, my partner, or my financial/health/security data** → private skill (`_ALLCAPS`).

**When in doubt, build it private first (`_ALLCAPS`). Promoting `_FOO` → `Foo` later is easy. Discovering a public skill leaks your life is permanent.**

---

## Public Release Readiness (MANDATORY)

**Public skills (`TitleCase`) ship to the world. Private skills (`_ALLCAPS`) never leave the local repo.** Sensitivity is decided by skill name, not by per-file scrubbing at share-time.

### The Bright Line

**Public skill (`TitleCase`) — content rule:**

ONLY templated, safe, public, ready content. Period.

- ✅ Generic instructions any LifeOS user could follow
- ✅ Templated patterns with placeholders for user-specific values
- ✅ Public API references and dependencies on public tools
- ❌ Real names (people, products, companies, customers)
- ❌ Real domains, hostnames, IPs, internal URLs
- ❌ API keys, tokens, credentials, session cookies, OAuth secrets — even example-looking ones
- ❌ Private repo paths or references (`github.com/<org>/<private-repo>`)
- ❌ Customer data, customer-specific workflows, customer engagement context
- ❌ First-person war stories tied to a specific incident, project, or person
- ❌ User-specific filesystem paths (`/Users/<name>/...`, `/home/<name>/...`)
- ❌ Identity-bound preferences (DA name, principal name, partner name, pet name, financial figures, health data)

**Private skill (`_ALLCAPS`) — content rule:**

Anything goes. Real names, real domains, real customers, real credentials-by-reference (env var names, never values), real war stories, real internal infra. The underscore IS the safety boundary. These skills are excluded from release tooling.

### The Decision Test

When you find yourself wanting to write any of the following into a skill body, that skill MUST be `_ALLCAPS`:

| If the skill mentions… | Skill must be |
|------------------------|---------------|
| A specific person's name (yours, your partner's, your team's, a customer's) | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific product name you own or sell | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific customer or client | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific paid API account, billing realm, or subscription | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific private domain, hostname, internal IP, or VPN | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific private repo, dotfile location, or local infra | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific business process tied to your company | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific financial, health, security, or legal context | `_ALLCAPS` |
| A specific incident or one-off war story | `_ALLCAPS` |
| Anything that would be wrong, embarrassing, or unsafe in someone else's `~/.claude/` | `_ALLCAPS` |

If none of the above apply and the skill is fully generic — it can be `TitleCase` (public).

### Where Personal Layering Goes for Public Skills

A public skill can be made user-specific at runtime via `~/.claude/LIFEOS/USER/CUSTOMIZATIONS/SKILLS/<SkillName>/PREFERENCES.md`. The skill body stays generic; the user's customization file overlays per-instance context. Use this when a skill is fundamentally generic but benefits from per-user tweaks (preferred voice, default formats, personal taste).

**Do not use SKILLCUSTOMIZATIONS to smuggle private content into a public skill.** If the skill *requires* private context to function (real customer name, real API account, real internal infra), it is a private skill — name it `_ALLCAPS` and stop.

### Allowed in Public Skills

- Generic `~/` paths (`~/.claude/skills/`, `~/Projects/<tool>/`) — resolve per-user
- Public repo URLs for tools the skill depends on
- Public API endpoints that are conventions, not secrets (e.g., `localhost:31337/notify`)
- Example values clearly marked as placeholders (`<url>`, `<SESSION_ID>`, `test@example.com`)
- Generic env var *names* (never values): `STRIPE_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`

### Pre-Flight Grep (Public Skills Only)

Before shipping or modifying any `TitleCase` skill, run:
```bash
rg -i "<your-name>|<your-org>|<your-product>|<your-domain>|/Users/[a-z]+/" ~/.claude/skills/<SkillName>/
```

Zero matches = ready for public release. Any match = either scrub it, move it to SKILLCUSTOMIZATIONS, or rename the skill to `_ALLCAPS` and stop pretending it's public. **`_ALLCAPS` skills are exempt from this grep — they are private by design.**

---

## Flat Folder Structure (MANDATORY)

**CRITICAL: Keep folder structure FLAT - maximum 2 levels deep.**

### The Rule

**Maximum depth:** `skills/SkillName/Category/`

### ✅ ALLOWED (2 levels max)

```
skills/SkillName/SKILL.md                    # Skill root
skills/SkillName/Workflows/Create.md         # Workflow - one level deep - GOOD
skills/SkillName/Tools/Manage.ts             # Tool - one level deep - GOOD
skills/SkillName/QuickStartGuide.md          # Context file - in root - GOOD
skills/SkillName/Examples.md                 # Context file - in root - GOOD
```

### ❌ FORBIDDEN (Too deep OR wrong location)

```
skills/SkillName/Resources/Guide.md              # Context files go in root, NOT Resources/
skills/SkillName/Docs/Examples.md                # Context files go in root, NOT Docs/
skills/SkillName/Workflows/Category/File.md      # THREE levels - NO
skills/SkillName/Templates/Primitives/File.md    # THREE levels - NO
skills/SkillName/Tools/Utils/Helper.ts           # THREE levels - NO
```

### Allowed Subdirectories

**These subdirectories are allowed:**
- **Workflows/** - Execution workflows ONLY
- **Tools/** - Executable scripts/tools ONLY
- **References/** - Extended reference material for large skills (API docs, detailed guides)

**Context files (documentation, guides, references) go in the skill ROOT or in References/.**

**When to use References/:** When SKILL.md exceeds ~500 lines and has substantial reference content (API signatures, detailed examples, troubleshooting guides). Keep SKILL.md as a routing guide; move encyclopedic content to References/.

### Why

1. **Discoverability** - Easy to find files
2. **Simplicity** - Less navigation overhead
3. **Speed** - Faster file operations
4. **Consistency** - Every skill follows same pattern

**If you need to organize many workflows, use clear filenames instead of subdirectories:**

**See:** `~/.claude/LIFEOS/DOCUMENTATION/Skills/SkillSystem.md` (Flat Folder Structure section)

---

## Dynamic Loading Pattern (Large Skills)

**For skills with SKILL.md > 100 lines:** Use dynamic loading to reduce context on skill invocation.

### How Loading Works

**Session startup:** Only frontmatter loads for routing
**Skill invocation:** Full SKILL.md loads
**Context files:** Load only when workflows reference them

### The Pattern

**SKILL.md** = Minimal (30-50 lines) - loads on skill invocation
- YAML frontmatter with triggers
- Brief description
- Workflow routing table
- Quick reference
- Pointers to context files

**Additional .md files** = Context files - SOPs for specific aspects (loaded on-demand)
- These are Standard Operating Procedures, not just documentation
- They provide specific handling instructions
- Can reference Workflows/, Tools/, etc.

### 🚨 CRITICAL: NO Context/ Subdirectory 🚨

**NEVER create Context/ or Docs/ subdirectories.**

Additional .md files ARE the context files. They live **directly in skill root**.

**WRONG:**
```
skills/Art/
├── SKILL.md
└── Context/              ❌ NEVER CREATE THIS
    └── Aesthetic.md
```

**CORRECT:**
```
skills/Art/
├── SKILL.md
├── Aesthetic.md          ✅ Context file in skill root
├── Examples.md           ✅ Context file in skill root
└── Tools.md              ✅ Context file in skill root
```

**The skill directory IS the context.**

### Example Structure

```
skills/Art/
├── SKILL.md              # 40 lines - minimal routing
├── Aesthetic.md          # Context file - SOP for aesthetic
├── Examples.md           # Context file - SOP for examples
├── Tools.md              # Context file - SOP for tools
├── Workflows/            # Workflows
│   └── Essay.md
└── Tools/                # CLI tools
    └── Generate.ts
```

### Minimal SKILL.md Template

```markdown
---
name: SkillName
description: Create, test, and optimize LifeOS skills — scaffolding, effectiveness testing, description optimization. USE WHEN create skill, new skill, validate skill, test skill, improve skill, optimize description.
---

# SkillName

Brief description.

## Workflow Routing

| Trigger | Workflow |
|---------|----------|
| "trigger" | `Workflows/WorkflowName.md` |

## Quick Reference

**Key points** (3-5 bullet points)

**Full Documentation:**
- Detail 1: `SkillSearch('skillname detail1')` → loads Detail1.md
- Detail 2: `SkillSearch('skillname detail2')` → loads Detail2.md
```

### When To Use

✅ **Use dynamic loading for:**
- SKILL.md > 100 lines
- Multiple documentation sections
- Extensive API reference
- Detailed examples

❌ **Don't use for:**
- Simple skills (< 50 lines)
- Pure utility wrappers (use LIFEOS/TOOLS.md instead)

### Benefits

- **Token Savings:** 70%+ reduction on skill invocation (when full docs not needed)
- **Organization:** SKILL.md = routing, context files = SOPs for specific aspects
- **Efficiency:** Workflows load only what they actually need
- **Maintainability:** Easier to update individual sections

**See:** `~/.claude/LIFEOS/DOCUMENTATION/Skills/SkillSystem.md` (Dynamic Loading Pattern section)

---


## Workflow Routing

### Structure Workflows (scaffolding and conventions)

| Workflow | Trigger | File |
|----------|---------|------|
| **CreateSkill** | "create a new skill" | `Workflows/CreateSkill.md` |
| **ValidateSkill** | "validate skill", "check skill" | `Workflows/ValidateSkill.md` |
| **UpdateSkill** | "update skill", "add workflow" | `Workflows/UpdateSkill.md` |
| **CanonicalizeSkill** | "canonicalize", "fix skill structure" | `Workflows/CanonicalizeSkill.md` |

### Effectiveness Workflows (testing and optimization)

| Workflow | Trigger | File |
|----------|---------|------|
| **TestSkill** | "test skill", "does this skill work", "skill not working" | `Workflows/TestSkill.md` |
| **ImproveSkill** | "improve skill", "skill quality", "fix skill instructions" | `Workflows/ImproveSkill.md` |
| **OptimizeDescription** | "optimize description", "skill not triggering", "trigger accuracy" | `Workflows/OptimizeDescription.md` |

## Skill Types (Choose Before Building)

Before creating any skill, identify which of the 9 types it is (from Anthropic's internal skill taxonomy, Thariq Shihipar, Mar 2026). The type shapes structure and testing decisions.

| Type | Focus | Key Structure | Example |
|------|-------|---------------|---------|
| 1. Library/API Reference | Gotchas, edge cases Claude gets wrong | Lightweight, gotchas-heavy, reference snippets | HonoReference, D1Reference |
| 2. Product Validation | Test/verify code works | State assertions, browser automation, output recording | Browser |
| 3. Data Fetching | Connect to data systems | Credential refs, query patterns, dashboard pointers | USMetrics, _METRICS |
| 4. Business Process | Automate repetitive workflows | Execution logs, consistency tracking | _CLICKUP, _BROADCAST |
| 5. Code Scaffolding | Generate framework boilerplate | Template files, project-aware scripts | CreateCLI, CreateSkill |
| 6. Code Quality | Enforce standards, review | Deterministic scripts, hook integration | /simplify, /code-review |
| 7. CI/CD & Deployment | Deploy with safety patterns | Pre-deploy checks, smoke tests, rollback | (gap — needs Deploy skill) |
| 8. Operations Runbooks | Map phenomena to diagnostics | Phenomenon → tool → query → report | _HEALTHCHECK |
| 9. Infrastructure Ops | Maintenance with safety guardrails | Safety gates, audit logging, orphan detection | _LIFEOS, _DOTFILES |

## Skill Writing Guidance

When writing or improving skill instructions, follow these principles from Anthropic's skill-creator methodology and Thariq Shihipar's "Lessons from Building Claude Code" (Mar 2026):

### Core Principles

- **Don't state the obvious.** Claude is competent at programming and knows codebases. Focus on information that **breaks Claude's default patterns** — things it gets wrong without guidance. Test: "Would Claude do this wrong without being told?" If not, remove it.
- **Explain the why, not just the what.** Models with good theory of mind + clear reasoning outperform models with rigid constraints. Instead of "ALWAYS use 3 bullets", explain why bullets matter for the audience.
- **Keep it lean.** The context window is a public good. Remove instructions that don't improve output. If test transcripts show the agent wasting time on unproductive steps, cut them. SKILL.md should be under 500 lines.
- **Cut intensifier-only lines.** Stating a rule once is the instruction. `MANDATORY`, `CRITICAL`, "not optional", and a third restatement add volume, not constraint — the model obeys specificity and code, not emphasis. Delete any line whose only content is shouting a rule stated elsewhere. Watch `## Best Practices` / `## Tips` sections: they collect default-restating filler ("be thorough", "keep it simple", "validate carefully"). Run the delete-test in `Prompting/Standards.md` § Signal-to-Noise on every line: cut it, and restore only if you can name the specific non-default behavior it forces.
- **Generalize, don't overfit.** Fix underlying patterns, not specific test failures. The skill will be used on many prompts beyond your test set.
- **Bundle repeated work.** If test agents all independently wrote similar helper scripts, add that script to Tools/ so every future invocation benefits.
- **Set appropriate degrees of freedom.** Match specificity to task fragility. Database migrations need exact commands; code reviews need general direction.
- **Don't over-constrain.** Skills are reused heavily. Avoid overly specific instructions. Provide needed information but leave flexibility for different contexts.

### Description Best Practices

- **Descriptions are for models, not humans.** The description is injected into the system prompt. Claude reads it to decide whether to invoke the skill.
- **Descriptions should be slightly pushy.** Models tend to undertrigger. Name specific scenarios even if the user might not explicitly mention the skill.
- **Include negative triggers for confusable skills.** Add "NOT FOR" clauses when skills share vocabulary: `"NOT FOR web pentesting (use WebAssessment)"`.
- **Undertriggering signals:** Skill doesn't load when it should, users manually invoking it.
- **Overtriggering signals:** Skill loads for irrelevant queries, users disabling it.

### Gotchas Section (MANDATORY)

Every skill MUST have a `## Gotchas` section after the workflow routing table. Thariq: "The highest information density in any Skill comes from gotchas sections."

Populate with:
- API quirks Claude doesn't know about
- Common mistakes observed during usage
- Ordering/sequencing requirements that aren't obvious
- Edge cases that cause silent failures

**Gotchas accumulate over time.** After every skill failure, add the lesson.

### BPE (Bitter-Pilled Engineering) Check

Before finalizing any skill, ask: **"Would a smarter model make this skill unnecessary?"**

- **Anti-fragile (keep):** Verification harnesses, data pipelines, tool wrappers, accumulated gotchas, deterministic scripts
- **Fragile (question):** CoT orchestrators, format parsers, retry cascades, elaborate reasoning scaffolding

Focus skills on knowledge Claude can't derive (failure modes, API quirks), tools Claude can't replicate (API calls, automation), and workflows that benefit from consistency.

### Progressive Disclosure (from Anthropic)

Three levels of information loading — use this to manage large skills:
1. **Level 1 (YAML frontmatter):** Always in system prompt. Triggering info only.
2. **Level 2 (SKILL.md body):** Loaded when skill is invoked. Routing + key guidance.
3. **Level 3 (Reference files):** Root-level `.md` files or `References/` subdirectory loaded on demand.

Tell Claude what files exist; it will read them when appropriate. SKILL.md should be under 500 lines — if over, extract detailed content to reference files.

### Testing Best Practices (from Anthropic)

Three testing levels for skills:
1. **Manual testing** — Run queries and observe behavior
2. **Scripted testing** — Automate test cases (use TestSkill workflow)
3. **Programmatic testing** — Build evaluation suites (use Evals skill)

**Evaluation-driven development:** Define what "this skill working" looks like before building the skill. Iterate on a single challenging task until Claude succeeds, then extract the winning approach.

### On-Demand Hook Pattern (from Anthropic)

Skills can include hooks that activate only when invoked, remaining effective for the session:
- `/careful` — Intercept dangerous commands (rm -rf, DROP TABLE, force-push)
- `/freeze` — Block edits outside specific directories
- `/audit` — Log all tool calls for session review

*All guidance above derived from Thariq Shihipar's "Lessons from Building Claude Code" (Mar 2026), Anthropic's official skill guide, and platform documentation.*

## Examples

**Example 1: Create a new skill from scratch**
```

---
name: memory-write
description: >
  Writes, updates, removes, and recalls facts in the two-tier memory system at
  ~/.claude/global-memory/ and ~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/. Use for write
  requests such as "remember this", "note that", "update memory", "save this",
  and "forget about", and for recall requests such as "did we already…?",
  "what did we decide about X?", and "do you remember…?". For writes, selects
  the correct tier and enforces deduplication and character caps. For recall,
  checks the injected snapshot first, then follows the memsearch retrieval ladder.
---

# Memory Write

## Outcome
- Fact added to, updated in, or removed from the correct memory tier
- Tier-B caps enforced (2,500 chars for MEMORY.md, 1,375 for USER.md)
- Confirmation: "Saved — will be active from next session."

## Pick the tier first

Ask: "Will this fact still be true and useful in 3 months, across multiple projects?"

**Tier A — `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`** (one file per fact, indexed by MEMORY.md)
- Durable user facts → `user_*.md` (metadata.type: user)
- Stable project conventions / gotchas → `project_*.md` (metadata.type: project)
- Behavioral feedback rules → `feedback_*.md` (metadata.type: feedback)
- External-system pointers → `reference_*.md` (metadata.type: reference)

**Tier B — `~/.claude/global-memory/`** (single capped file)
- Active threads (in-progress work) → `MEMORY.md` `## Active Threads`
- Current env notes (URLs, tool versions, project structure in play) → `MEMORY.md` `## Environment Notes`
- Pending decisions → `MEMORY.md` `## Pending Decisions`
- Durable user profile updates → `USER.md`

## Steps

1. **Decide tier** using the rule above.
2. **Read** the target file in full.
3. **Dedup check** — substring scan; if the fact already exists, skip or update in place.
4. **Cap check** for Tier B — `wc -c < ~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (or USER.md). If over cap, consolidate (merge similar entries, prune stale) before adding.
5. **Write** the change.
   - Tier A: create a new file with proper frontmatter (name, description, metadata.type) and add a one-line pointer to that slug's `MEMORY.md` index.
   - Tier B: append under the correct `##` section.
6. **Confirm** in one line: `Saved — will be active from next session.`

## Actions

- **add** — append (default)
- **replace** — substring match + swap. Preferred over add when updating an existing fact.
- **remove** — confirm with the user before deleting.

## Retrieval — the tiered ladder

When the user asks about past context, decisions, or "did we already…?", climb in order and stop as soon as the question is answered. Do not run memsearch when the answer is already in the injected snapshot.

1. **Tier 0** — scan what is already in context (USER.md, MEMORY.md, today's compiled log). Zero cost.
2. **L1** — `memsearch search "query" --top-k 5`. Hybrid vector + keyword across all indexed paths: Tier A files (including the retired Windows slugs), daily logs, transcripts.
3. **L2** — `memsearch expand <chunk_hash>`. Full markdown section around a hit.
4. **L3** — `memsearch transcript <session_id>`. Raw dialogue. Last resort.
5. **Fallback** — say "I don't have a record of that."

## Daily compiled logs — read-only

`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/{YYYY-MM-DD}.md` is produced by `claude-memory-compiler` through its own SessionEnd/PreCompact hooks, and injected by its own SessionStart hook.

- **Never hand-edit these files.** The compiler owns them.
- **Never read them eagerly.** Treat the injected snapshot as the source of truth.

## What is loaded at session start

`~/.claude/global-memory/USER.md` and `MEMORY.md` are read once at session start and are a **frozen snapshot**. Mid-session writes persist to disk but only take effect next session — this is deliberate, to preserve the prefix cache. Never load more than the startup set proactively.

## Rules

- Never exceed Tier B caps. Consolidate first.
- Always dedup before adding.
- For Tier A, the slug is the current cwd with `/` and `.` replaced by `-` (so `~` → `-Users-kristinarash`, `~/DEV` → `-Users-kristinarash-DEV`, `~/.claude/skills` → `-Users-kristinarash--claude-skills`). The harness injects the correct slug each session — use that, don't reconstruct it.
- **Never write to a `C--Users-eric-rash*` slug.** Those are pre-migration Windows keys from the box retired 2026-08-14. They are still indexed by memsearch, so old facts stay recallable, but nothing written there will ever be auto-injected again.
- Never announce the write mid-session beyond the one-line confirmation. The injected snapshot is frozen — the new fact appears next session, not this one.

decision; it does not substitute for it.

## Did it work

Yes. The memory checker went from **4 index errors + 37 broken links** to **0 errors, 0 warnings**. I proved the new check is not fake by breaking a file on purpose, watching it get caught, then putting it back.

## What I changed

**Names (option A).** 68 files renamed, 64 links repointed. The rule: `name:` is the filename minus the front tag. So `project_automation-cadence.md` gets `name: automation-cadence`. Only the *front* tag comes off, so `feedback_project_idea_capture.md` keeps its `project`.

**Klanderman.** Fixed in the 2 real notes.

**4 hidden files.** They were on disk but not in the index, so no session ever loaded them. Two are your OKR gate items, and that gate date has passed. Now indexed.

**Built gap 3 — proposals stop vanishing.**
`~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/reports/proposals-pending.md`
One list. Each item says open / approved / rejected / applied. `session-miner` and `improve-system` now read it *before* proposing. You still approve everything. Nothing is auto-applied.

**Built gap 2 — mining the real record.**
`session-miner` can now read the raw `.jsonl` session files, not just the summaries. It writes no new parser — two already existed. Hard caps so it cannot bankrupt you: 14 days, 20 sessions, ~200 KB each, tool output stripped, subagent only. It also carries a line saying DexaProject health data must never leave the subagent.

**Guard rail.** The rule is now written into `memory-write`, and memlint has a new **Name form** check. Sunday's job will catch it if the split starts again.

## One thing was a false alarm

**The compiler backlog is not real.** I had it wrong at first. `daily/` is what the compiler *reads*, not what it writes. Those 8 old days simply have no daily log — the compiler never ran then. A dry run shows only today pending, which is normal. **No action needed. I spent nothing.**

## What you do now

The compiler repo is on a branch, **committed but not pushed**:

```

cd ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler && gh pr create --base main --head memlint-memory-tier-checks --title "feat: memlint.py — health checks for the memory tier" --body-file - <<'EOF'
`lint.py` only ever covered the knowledge base. `memlint.py` covers the tier that
nothing checked: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the active
`~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs.

**Report-only by design.** It never edits a memory file. Memory deletion is gated on a
user confirmation by the `memory-write` skill, and this tool does not get to route
around that.

Wired to run after `adjudicate.py` in the Sunday 02:30 job.

## Seven checks

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | A memory file missing from `MEMORY.md`, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` matching no frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into `MEMORY.md`, which holds pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims |

## Result on the real corpus

Contradictions went 34 → 17 after the first cleanup. The second pass took the
structural checks from **4 index errors + 37 broken links to 0 errors, 0 warnings**
(9 suggestions remain, all deliberate placeholders for memories not written yet).

## The non-obvious choices

- **Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere.** The macOS slugs were
  re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication (~30 false
  pairs). Matched case-insensitively — a `c--` variant exists on disk too.
- **The 0.45 near-duplicate threshold was measured, not guessed.** On the real corpus
  the highest genuine within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top
  pairs per slug so it can be retuned against evidence rather than taste.
- **Similarity is within-slug only.** Cross-slug pairs are noise by design.
- **`--structural-only` writes `memlint-<date>-structural.md`**, so a free run cannot
  clobber the day's paid-for LLM findings. That footgun was hit three times before it
  was fixed.

## Why `Name form` exists

`name:` had no stated rule, so both spellings looked correct in isolation. An audit
found the corpus split 59 bare / 58 prefixed, and that split had broken 37 links —
links resolve against `name:`, so a file declaring the wrong form is unreachable from
every note pointing at it.

The rule is now written into the `memory-write` skill: `name:` is the filename stem
minus its **leading** type token, kebab-cased. Only the leading one, so
`feedback_project_idea_capture.md` keeps `project` in its name. This check enforces it
on the Sunday run so the split cannot regrow silently. Files with no `name:` field are
skipped — that is a different defect.

Verified by negative test: reverting one file to the prefixed form is caught, and
restoring it clears.

## Scope

Touches `scripts/memlint.py` (new), `scripts/config.py`, `scripts/weekly-adjudicate.ps1`,
`README.md`, `AGENTS.md`. Pre-existing uncommitted changes to `hooks/session-start.py`,
`scripts/flush.py` and `uv.lock` were left alone — they are not from this work.
